particulars: All names, dates, places, ages, sentence lengths, stab-wound counts, deadlines and governors' names are dropped.

items.record: The case centers on one man wrongly convicted and sentenced to death: "The jurors returned with their verdict of death."
items.reading: Describes an official public statement to the general population that responds to a growing fringe movement or counter-narrative.
items.loss: The basic nature of the case is wrong: it is a criminal prosecution of an individual, not a public communication dispute.

items.record: Police extracted a coerced, false confession from a suspect held on an unrelated charge: "After two days of questioning, police claimed he had 'confessed' to a total of five different crimes."
items.loss: The mechanism that produced the injustice, a manufactured confession under custodial pressure, is missing.

items.record: The confession was rehearsed and shaped by police until it was acceptable: "Only on the fourth attempt at a rehearsed confession did authorities accept Washington's statement."
items.loss: The step-by-step process by which authorities built the evidence they then relied on is missing.

items.record: The suspect's account contradicted the known facts on race, height, wounds and the children present: "Washington did not know the race of his victim... or that he had raped her."
items.loss: The visible gap between the confession and reality, which authorities overlooked, is missing.

items.record: Police guided the suspect to the crime scene: "taken there three times in one afternoon by the police, who in the end had to help him pick out Williams' apartment."
items.loss: The way officials fed the suspect the knowledge he was supposed to have is missing.

items.record: His intellectual disability made him defer to anyone in authority: "Washington would politely defer to any authority figure with whom he came into contact."
items.reading: Treats the audience as atomized individuals weighing a broadcast, with low solidarity.
items.loss: The extreme power imbalance between a vulnerable individual and the state, and how that vulnerability was exploited, is missing.

items.record: Forensic evidence that cleared him was rewritten without new testing: "an amended forensic report was prepared (without additional testing being conducted) that said testing for the rare protein was 'inconclusive.'"
items.reading: Reads the authority's statement as "clear, relevant and not deceptive in its particulars" and leans toward the authority being right on the facts.
items.loss: Deliberate falsification of evidence by the institution is reversed into presumed honesty.

items.record: The trial was one-sided, with only the state's expert testifying on competence and no defense case at sentencing: "the defense did not offer any counter argument to the jury concerning a sentence of death."
items.loss: The failure of the adversarial process and of defense counsel is missing.

items.record: Rescue came through informal help from other prisoners and volunteers: "another death row inmate... alerted Marie Deans (a non-lawyer...) and a lawyer who was at the Virginia prison working on another case."
items.reading: Says the fringe offers belonging and that resolution would need engagement or transparency.
items.loss: The chance network of fellow inmates, a volunteer and outside lawyers who intervened at the last moment is missing.

items.record: A stay came just before execution: "secured a stay of execution for Washington nine days before he was scheduled to die."
items.loss: The life-or-death stakes and the narrow timing of the intervention are missing.

items.record: Procedural rules blocked exoneration even after DNA excluded him: "Because Washington was time barred by Virginia law... he was not exonerated. Instead... commuted Washington's sentence to life imprisonment."
items.reading: Assumes the institution suppresses the dispute and holds to its account.
items.loss: The way legal deadlines kept an innocent man imprisoned, and the state's partial concession through commutation, is missing.

items.record: Correction came in stages over years through executive clemency: a limited pardon, release to parole, then "an absolute pardon, which acknowledged that Washington was wrongfully convicted."
items.reading: Predicts the conflict does not resolve, hardens, and the institution's account persists.
items.loss: The actual outcome, a slow, step-by-step official admission of error, is misdescribed.

items.record: The real perpetrator was identified: "Kenneth Tinsley... pleaded guilty to Rebecca Lynn Williams' rape and murder."
items.loss: The final resolution of who was actually responsible is missing.

items.record: The exonerated man responded mildly to freedom: "This was a whole lot better than I expected."
items.reading: Imagines officials feeling responsible and frustrated, and fringe members feeling vindicated.
items.loss: The experience of the wrongly convicted person himself is missing.

items.record: The trigger was a violent crime with a vague victim description: "She could only describe her attacker as a Black man acting alone."
items.reading: Says the trigger was a fast-growing fringe conflict.
items.loss: The originating event, and the racial vagueness that let suspicion fall on an arbitrary person, is misidentified.
